column1: # Junk-title rules — the shipped defaults, a FULL port of prod's
# whichJunkPattern / whichJunkPatternSized (prod is the source of truth; names,
# thresholds and ORDER match prod exactly, so hit counters are comparable).
# This file is the SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH: it is embedded in the binary (so the
# filter works with no database), and it seeds the junk_rules table on boot. The
# live filter is then loaded from that table into memory, so operators can add,
# tune, or disable rules without a code release. Rules run in THIS order.
# One rule per line so diffs are per-rule and a community PR adding a pattern
# reads as one line. Tab-separated. Lines starting with # are comments.
#   name    stable identifier (prod's pattern name), reported when a rule fires
#   rule    kind=regex: the pattern. kind=heuristic: the built-in algorithm id.
#   params  JSON object; {} when unused. Recognised keys:
#           A rule with a size bound fires ONLY when the caller knows the
#           release size (the build path) — never on per-article ingest.
# Obfuscated posts use random-token subjects that would otherwise assemble into
# garbage "releases". PATTERNS are what generalise here — a denylist of seen
# subjects is useless, because every obfuscated post is a fresh random string.

column5: notes
24+ consecutive alphanumerics anywhere = a hash or token. The workhorse rule.

2+ segments (split on _ or space) of 5+ chars that each mix upper, lower AND digit, in an alnum+underscore+space-only title. Each segment sits at 20-23 chars so long_alnum_run never sees a single 24+ run.

A canonical UUID anywhere in the title. The 8-4-4-4-12 shape never appears in real release names. Boundary-less on purpose: \b missed underscore-adjacent uuids ("Upload_<uuid>" — the agent's obfuscated posts), which prod's SQL sweep (also boundary-less) always caught.

Cracked-software boilerplate, curated product names, (x64)/(x86) markers, 4-part version strings, and the bare "input" full-title spam. Anime-only catalog: a 200 MB installer is junk regardless of size.

Leftover poster-template tokens the poster never substituted: {total}, {{count}}. Single-brace form is LOWERCASE-only on purpose: template placeholders are lowercase identifiers, while braces in a release name are operator tags -- {REDO}, {DVD}, {RAW} -- and the uppercase form was dropping a real 4xDVD9 Gundam post. The {{...}} form stays case-insensitive; nothing names a release that way.
Dot-separated obfuscated pair like f329yZ98AaYf2qHd.QPv2 — only when it mixes case AND digits, so real short names survive.
ROT13'd software cracks / DVD rips: .ene = .rar rot13'd, cerfragf = "presents", CNFFJBEQ = "PASSWORD", plus known rot13'd poster handles.
The same 2-20 char alnum token repeated twice ("rtNJ rtNJ"). Programmatic: RE2 has no backreferences. Tokens over 5 chars must mix digit+letter so "New York New York" shapes stay safe.
<blob>.<ext> with no other separators — "07w5a8eborq1saw8zg.1v8". Not always mixed-case, so dot_sep_obfuscated misses the all-lowercase variants.
Bare 6-15 char alnum token with BOTH digit and letter — "S7rEx773", "0N70ZyFoz8n50". The digit gate spares pure-letter titles (Lamune, Gunbuster). Prod's single largest junk class (34k+ rows).
Bare 16-19 char token, same digit+letter gate — "pE9F9wMjNxWZqpq9V". Fills the gap between short_alnum_token and single_token_20.
Unevaluated ${...} template literal — a poster's templating engine leaked its source. Real titles never contain ${...}.
A single pure-alnum token of 20+ chars with no separators: dashless UUIDs, 40/56/60-char hashes, base64 blobs. No digit gate — no real title is a bare 20+ run at all.

A band-shaped token wearing the poster's size annotation: "rP8nmcYiqE2eAjw7 - 49,37 GB". The tail defeats every bare-token rule, sized ones included, so these indexed at any size. Measured 2026-08-08: 692 bases / 471,563 articles in one staging window — 6.2% of everything the rest of the engine passes — vs ONE hit in 81,416 catalogued titles, itself this family. Head reuses the band gates (6+, digit+letter under 20), so pure-letter and punctuated real names survive by the same rules that spare them bare. Placed after its band siblings: decline cost is a last-byte compare, and below this slot sit gateless regexes every caught article would otherwise pay.
10+ consecutive digits = a Unix timestamp or hash fragment. Years are 4 digits, episode numbers <=4, IMDb ids are tt-prefixed.

The WHOLE title is digits once extensions are peeled: "700177022.bin", "82020282-n". Sits AFTER long_digit_run deliberately: that rule (10+ digits anywhere) already owns the 10-and-over bare titles in prod, and moving them here would reattribute existing hit counters for no functional gain -- both rules filter. This one covers the 6-9 digit gap neither reaches: long_digit_run's floor is 10, and short_alnum_token's digit gate wants a digit AND a letter, which spares pure-letter titles by design and pure-DIGIT ones by accident. Measured on production 2026-08-04: 39,404 of the newest 50,000 releases, 6.2 TB, none junk-tagged, none matchable, and 0 of 60 sampled NZBs carried a recoverable name inside. 6-digit floor: "86" is 2 chars, a year is 4.
15%+ of the title is spam-grade punctuation. Release separators (.-_()[] space) and angle brackets are allowed — <<<Nimue>>> signature wrapping is legitimate.
Random alnum words (8+ chars mixing digits and letters) make up 70%+ of the non-punct chars — one 12+ char word or several totalling 16+.
node_one_7bd4f69e lowercase word/word/8-hex spam, gated under 10 MiB so a big legit release that coincidentally matches is spared.

Any no-whitespace title under ~790 KB — the May-2026 6.8M-row spam wave, uniformly ~740 KB. "Legit tiny NZBs always have spaces in their titles" was the original reasoning and it does not survive a catalogue with subtitles and single tracks in it: those are dotted filenames with no spaces at all, which is why spare_named_media is set. It still fires on the wave, whose titles are bare tokens.
12-20 char pure-lowercase bare token under 1 MiB — "wardcfsejnodpdci" bot variants sitting just above the tiny_no_space cutoff.
60+ chars, no whitespace, 5+ spam-grade punct, small payload. The punct guard spares legit dot-separated names like Beyonce.-.I.Am... (at real sizes).

60+ chars, no whitespace, 8+ spam-grade punct, ANY size. Closes the gap long_no_space leaves above its 2 MiB cap and on the unsized ingest path: a 111-char random-string post scored 18 marks and matched no rule at all above 5 MiB. Bar is a COUNT (8) not a ratio, because high_special_chars' 15% ratio missed that title at 14.4%. Measured against the live catalogue: of 200 titles with 60+ chars and no whitespace, ZERO carry 8+ marks and zero carry even 4, so this touches nothing real. Dot-separated names (Beyonce.-.I.Am...) score 0 because '.' and '-' are not spam-grade.
The whitespace-allowed sibling: 30+ chars WITH whitespace, 3+ spam-grade punct, small payload — the ")yury0Wgt... k2cwcKzuD!" 723 KB wave.

Orphan PAR2 recovery-volume post ("sigma-sun.vol024+02"): a single-file-form subject names only the volume, so it never groups under its parent release and indexes as a payload-free "release". The .par2 tail is normally pre-stripped by ext peeling; the optional branch covers raw titles.
Bare 8-19 char mixed-case alnum token, ANY size — production caught "XIfhyEYhXpZaXTVK" at 433 MB; a bare mixed-case run has no legit release-naming analogue.

Catchall: anything under 1 MiB that survived every specific rule AND does not name a media type this size is normal for. The original rule read "a sub-1 MiB NZB is never legitimate", which was true of an anime-only catalog and stopped being true when the site started collecting books, music and manga — see spare_named_media. Last real catch: "elys-1907283e54a1cae9 - [KXPSbTzl] qoS5w5nwO0OvHnwj".

Catchall for the 1-5 MiB band, where the word_word_hex bot wave lives. Ordered last so the specific rules above get attribution credit. spare_named_media is NOT optional here: this band is where an ebook, a comic chapter and a single track all live, and the rule's last catch before it was added was "Blackthorn - J.T. Geissinger.epub" — a real book deleted for being 2 MB.
